result: Colon cancer is a major global health burden with significant incidence, mortality, and metastatic potential. In 2020, there were over 1 million new cases and 500,000 deaths globally, with 19-26% of patients presenting with synchronous metastatic disease at diagnosis, including 14.5-17.5% developing liver metastasis. The 2-year survival rate for distant-stage disease is 36%, significantly lower than non-metastatic cases.
evaluation: Claims C1-C6 are all supported by appropriate citations to published literature (Sung et al., 2021; Siegel et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2023). These claims establish the clinical context and significance of the study, providing well-documented epidemiological background from reputable sources.

result: The tumor microenvironment (TME) is a dynamic environment governing tumor behavior and is required for tumor cell survival, growth, proliferation, and metastasis. Recent evidence suggests certain immune cells in the TME, including myeloid-derived suppressor cells, macrophages, neutrophils, and CD8+ T cells, can favor tumor progression.
evaluation: Claims C7-C12 are supported by citations to relevant literature (Yao et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2023; Ngambenjawong et al., 2017; Li et al., 2019; Tiberti et al., 2022). These claims provide appropriate background on TME biology and the dual roles of immune cells, establishing the rationale for investigating NK cell heterogeneity.

result: NK cells are cytotoxic lymphocytes that play key roles in recognizing and eliminating malignant cells and are considered early responders against tumors. Tumor-infiltrating NK cells are associated with prognosis in various cancers including colorectal, lung, and gastric cancer. While NK cells show promise for treating hematologic malignancies, they have limited efficacy for solid tumors. Intratumor NK cells differ phenotypically and functionally from peripheral NK cells, with specific subsets (CD11b−CD27− and decidual-like CD9+CD49a+) associated with tumor progression. The tumor-promoting transformation of NK cells may be educated by cancer cells.
evaluation: Claims C13-C23 are well-supported by appropriate citations to published literature (Maskalenko et al., 2022; Zhong et al., 2022; Villegas et al., 2002; Ishigami et al., 2000; Lamb et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2024; Hu et al., 2019; Oh et al., 2019; Bruno et al., 2013; Carrega et al., 2008; Zhang et al., 2017; Jin et al., 2013; Albini and Noonan, 2021; Chan et al., 2020; Huergo-Zapico et al., 2018). These claims establish comprehensive background on NK cell biology and heterogeneity, providing strong rationale for the study.

result: Single-cell RNA-sequencing analysis of 178,630 CD45+ cells from CCLM samples identified major immune cell populations including monocytes, neutrophils, B cells, plasma cells, T cells, and NK cells. T and NK cells were the major immune cell components, with NK cells significantly decreasing in tumor tissues compared to adjacent normal tissues, while T cells showed the opposite pattern.
evaluation: Claims C24-C28 are supported by the text and referenced figures (Figure 1B-E, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A-C). The data analysis methods are described, and the findings are visualized in the figures. The observation of differential NK and T cell distributions across tissue types is clearly demonstrated and forms a key finding of the study.

result: Spatial transcriptomics analysis identified six morphological regions in CCLM samples: tumor, fibroblast, smooth muscle, B cells, hepatocytes, normal epithelium, and tumor/paratumor areas. Consistent with scRNA-seq, T cells were enriched in tumor regions while NK cells were enriched in non-tumor areas of both primary colon cancer and liver metastasis.
evaluation: Claims C29-C31 are supported by the text and referenced figures (Figure 2A-D, Figure 2—figure supplement 2). The spatial transcriptomics data corroborates the scRNA-seq findings and provides spatial context for immune cell distributions. The methodology combining H&E staining with gene expression features is appropriate for identifying morphological regions.

result: Bulk RNA-seq analysis using multiple deconvolution methods (MCPcounter, EPIC, xCell) showed decreased NK cell percentages in metastatic colon cancer. DEG analysis identified 1378 differentially expressed genes (817 upregulated, 561 downregulated) between metastatic and non-metastatic colon cancer. GO and KEGG enrichment analyses revealed significant enrichment of NK cell-related pathways including cell killing, NK cell-mediated immunity, cytotoxicity, and activation. Nearly all genes in the NK cell-mediated cytotoxicity pathway were downregulated in metastatic tumors, and GSEA confirmed enrichment of NK cell-mediated cytotoxicity in non-metastatic tumors.
evaluation: Claims C32-C36 are supported by the text and referenced figures (Figure 3A-H). Multiple independent computational methods converge on the same conclusion regarding NK cell depletion in metastatic disease. The DEG analysis with appropriate cutoffs (|log FC| > 1.5, p < 0.05) and pathway enrichment analyses provide mechanistic insights. The consistency across methods strengthens the findings.

result: Unsupervised clustering identified eight NK cell subtypes, which were classified into three main categories: activated NK cells (expressing KIR2DL4, GPR183, GRP171, CD69, IFNG), resting NK cells (expressing GZMK, TTC38, CD160, PLEKNF1), and other NK cells. During disease progression from normal colon to primary tumor to liver metastasis, resting NK cells increased while activated NK cells decreased.
evaluation: Claims C37-C44 are supported by the text and referenced figures (Figure 4A-H, Supplementary file 3-4). The classification of NK cells using CIBERSORT-reported markers is appropriate, and the progressive changes across disease stages are clearly demonstrated. The use of paired samples strengthens the conclusions about NK cell dynamics during progression.

result: Validation in TCGA COAD cohort using CIBERSORT confirmed that resting NK cells significantly increased while activated NK cells decreased in metastatic tumors and higher TNM stages. Resting NK cells and neutrophils were associated with worse prognosis, while activated NK cells and M1 macrophages were associated with better outcomes. Survival analysis in TCGA COAD and GSE29623 cohorts showed that higher resting NK cell infiltration and lower activated NK cell infiltration predicted significantly worse prognosis. Spatial transcriptomics confirmed resting NK cells were enriched in tumor regions while activated NK cells were enriched in non-tumor areas.
evaluation: Claims C45-C54 are supported by the text and referenced figures (Figure 5A-E, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A-B). The validation in independent cohorts (TCGA COAD and GSE29623) strengthens the findings. The survival analyses provide clinical relevance, and the spatial transcriptomics data corroborates the functional implications of NK cell subset distributions. The consistency across multiple datasets and methods is compelling.

result: KIR2DL4+ activated NK cells decreased while GZMK+ resting NK cells increased during disease progression from normal colon to colon cancer to liver metastasis. Spatial transcriptomics and mIHC confirmed differential infiltration patterns with KIR2DL4+ cells in non-tumor areas and GZMK+ cells in tumor regions. Pseudotime trajectory analysis revealed developmental routes beginning with KIR2DL4+ activated NK cells evolving into GZMK+ resting NK cells, with enrichment of leukocyte differentiation and immune system process-related GO terms. Higher GZMK+ resting NK cell infiltration and lower KIR2DL4+ activated NK cell infiltration were associated with shorter survival in TCGA COAD cohort.
evaluation: Claims C55-C63 are supported by the text and referenced figures (Figure 6A-H). The pseudotime trajectory analysis provides evidence for NK cell state transitions, and the mIHC validation in clinical samples strengthens the findings. The GO enrichment analysis of genes changing during the transition provides mechanistic insights. The survival associations add clinical relevance to the specific NK cell subsets identified.

result: In vitro co-culture experiments demonstrated that colon cancer cells cultured in supernatant from NK-tumor cell direct contact (CNS group) showed significantly increased proliferation, migration, and invasion compared to controls. NK cells exposed to tumor cells showed decreased KIR2DL4 expression, slightly increased GZMK expression, and increased expression of tumor-infiltrated NK cell markers (CD9, CD49a, PD-1), especially CD9. These phenotypic changes required direct cell-to-cell contact and were not observed with tumor supernatant or fresh medium alone.
evaluation: Claims C64-C70 are supported by the text and referenced figures (Figure 7A-Q). Multiple functional assays (CCK-8, colony formation, transwell migration/invasion) consistently demonstrate tumor-promoting effects. The FACS analysis provides evidence for NK cell phenotypic changes. The requirement for direct cell contact is well-controlled with appropriate comparison groups (SNS, MNS, CS). The experiments are appropriately replicated.

result: Luminex liquid suspension chip detection and ELISA confirmed that SCF was upregulated in the CNS group (NK-tumor cell direct contact supernatant). Imatinib mesylate (2 µM), a c-Kit inhibitor, significantly inhibited the supernatant-enhanced proliferation, migration, and invasion of HCT-116 cells.
evaluation: Claims C71-C74 are supported by the text and referenced figures (Figure 8A-M). The identification of SCF as a key mediator is supported by two independent methods (Luminex and ELISA). The functional validation using imatinib provides mechanistic evidence linking SCF/c-Kit signaling to the tumor-promoting effects. The experiments include appropriate controls (DMSO) and multiple functional assays.

result: No upregulation of KITLG (SCF-encoding gene) was found in HCT-116 after co-culturing with NK cells. DLD-1 cells, which have nearly 15 times lower KITLG expression than HCT-116, did not show tumor-promoting effects when cultured in co-culture supernatant.
evaluation: Claims C91-C93 are supported by the text and referenced figures (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A-B, Figure 7—figure supplement 1). The qPCR data showing no KITLG upregulation in HCT-116 and the negative results with DLD-1 cells provide important controls. These findings support the hypothesis that NK cells promote release of pre-existing membrane-bound SCF rather than inducing new SCF expression.

result: The authors hypothesize that NK cells promote cleavage and release of the extracellular part of SCF on tumor cell surfaces after direct contact, increasing sSCF concentration, which induces malignant phenotype of colon cancer cells in a paracrine manner.
evaluation: Claims C94-C95 represent a mechanistic hypothesis supported by multiple lines of evidence: (1) increased sSCF in CNS supernatant, (2) no KITLG upregulation in tumor cells, (3) requirement for direct cell contact, (4) differential effects in HCT-116 vs DLD-1 cells correlating with baseline KITLG expression, and (5) imatinib inhibition of tumor-promoting effects. While the exact mechanism of SCF cleavage is not directly demonstrated, the hypothesis is well-supported by the experimental data and is appropriately presented as a hypothesis (Figure 9).

result: The Discussion contextualizes the findings within existing literature on NK cell biology, TME remodeling, NK cell maturation states, tumor-associated NK cells, and SCF signaling. The authors appropriately cite relevant prior work and discuss how their findings align with or extend previous observations.
evaluation: Claims C75-C90, C104-C107 are all supported by appropriate citations to published literature. The Discussion appropriately integrates the current findings with prior knowledge, acknowledging both consistencies and novel aspects of the work. The citations are relevant and support the contextual claims made.

result: The abstract summarizes the main findings: GZMK+ resting NK cells increased in tumor tissues and were enriched in tumor regions, contributing to worse prognosis, while KIR2DL4+ activated NK cells showed opposite patterns. Pseudotime analysis revealed evolution from activated to resting NK cells. In vitro experiments confirmed tumor-cell-co-cultured NK cells exhibited decidual-like status with increased CD9 expression. NK cells exhibited tumor-activating characteristics by promoting SCF dissociation from tumor cell membranes via cell-to-cell interaction, with the co-culture supernatant enhancing tumor progression. Resting NK cells exhibited clinical relevance with CCLM.
evaluation: Claims C96-C103 accurately summarize the major findings presented in the Results section. Each claim in the abstract is supported by corresponding data and figures in the manuscript. The abstract appropriately represents the scope and conclusions of the study.
